# KOTOR, played together.

![KOTOR Co-op — an experimental co-op mod for Knights of the Old Republic](nexus/images/1-cover-title.jpg)

[![CI](https://github.com/ChristopherVR/kotor-coop/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/ChristopherVR/kotor-coop/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/ChristopherVR/kotor-coop)](https://github.com/ChristopherVR/kotor-coop/releases/latest)
[![License: GPL-3.0-only](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-GPL--3.0--only-blue)](LICENSE)
![Status: experimental beta](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-experimental_beta-orange)

**Your own character. A shared adventure. A friend beside you.**

A free, open-source co-op mod for **Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic**. One player hosts;
friends join the same world from their own copies of the game. Explore, fight and share the
story through the original game's menus, with a new **Co-op** button to bring you together.

**[Download the latest release](https://github.com/ChristopherVR/kotor-coop/releases/latest)** ·
[Get it on Nexus Mods](https://www.nexusmods.com/mod/1910) ·
[Watch the trailer](https://christophervr.github.io/kotor-coop/#trailer) ·
[Player guides](https://christophervr.github.io/kotor-coop/)

> **Experimental beta — start with two players and back up your saves.** Selected scenes have
> been tested on real game copies; a complete co-op campaign has not been verified. Up to eight
> players can connect, but larger-group campaign reliability remains experimental.

## See it in action

Real game footage, recorded using **two game copies on one PC** and disposable saves.
The menu, character, inventory, chat and reconnect clips were captured on **v0.1.0-beta.4**
using the background game harness. Cuts are labeled; each new GIF has a pauseable MP4.
The exploration, dialogue and combat clips come from our earlier
[gameplay trailer](https://christophervr.github.io/kotor-coop/#trailer).

### Host from the game menu

![Opening Co-op from KOTOR's main menu, choosing Host, then entering Dantooine after loading](site/media/showcase/host-from-menu.gif)

Open **Co-op → Host** to bring your save into a session. **Shown here:** starting a host in
the Jedi Enclave on Dantooine. The loading wait is cut from the loop.
[Watch or pause this clip](https://christophervr.github.io/kotor-coop/media/showcase/host-from-menu.mp4).

### Create your own character

![The joining player choosing a Soldier and cycling through portraits in KOTOR's character creator](site/media/showcase/create-character.gif)

A first-time join opens the game's character creator. **Shown here:** class and portrait
choices for the new Soldier who joined this session. The clip cuts between those two steps.
[Watch or pause this clip](https://christophervr.github.io/kotor-coop/media/showcase/create-character.mp4).

### Explore together

![Two connected players moving through Korriban, shown from both game copies](site/media/showcase/explore-together.gif)

See your friend as a character in the world. Walk together, follow each other through area changes,
and take the same trip between planets. **Shown here:** paired views of movement on Korriban.

### Share the conversation

![One player talking to Belaya while the second selects her and joins the same conversation](site/media/showcase/share-conversations.gif)

Whoever starts a conversation chooses the replies. The other player selects the same character
to watch; story-triggered scenes bring the party in automatically. **Shown here:** joining a
conversation with Belaya on Dantooine. One conversation runs at a time.

### Fight side by side

![Two players fighting the same kath hounds on Dantooine with blue and yellow lightsabers](site/media/showcase/fight-together.gif)

Fight shared enemies with your own character and gear. **Shown here:** blue and yellow sabers
against kath hounds on Dantooine. God mode was used for filming; this clip demonstrates shared
combat, not ordinary difficulty or balance.

### Your character. Your gear.

![Both players opening their own inventory and character sheets, with different portraits, items and stats](site/media/showcase/personal-inventory.gif)

Open your backpack and character sheet independently. **Shown here:** the established host
has gear, while the newly created Soldier has an empty backpack and his own stats.
[Watch or pause this clip](https://christophervr.github.io/kotor-coop/media/showcase/personal-inventory.mp4).

### Keep talking while you explore

![Player Two asking Ready to explore and Player One replying Ready, Lets go, with both messages visible in both game copies](site/media/showcase/in-game-chat.gif)

Messages appear inside both players' games. **Shown here:** a two-way chat exchange in the
Enclave courtyard, sent through the harness's console commands.
[Watch or pause this clip](https://christophervr.github.io/kotor-coop/media/showcase/in-game-chat.mp4).

### Leave and return

![The second player's character disappearing from the host's world on disconnect and returning after reconnecting](site/media/showcase/leave-and-rejoin.gif)

**Shown here:** Player Two disconnects and reconnects while the host stays in the courtyard.
The character disappears and returns in the host's view. This is a session reconnect with
both games still running; the loop cuts out the save and connection waits.
[Watch or pause this clip](https://christophervr.github.io/kotor-coop/media/showcase/leave-and-rejoin.mp4).

These staged clips illustrate selected features; a completed campaign and independent internet
playtest remain unverified. [New capture details](site/media/showcase/capture-20261030.json) ·
[Trailer capture details](site/media/provenance.json) ·
[GIF sources, edits and hashes](site/media/showcase/manifest.json).

## Install, host, connect

1. **Download** `kotor-coop-<version>-setup.exe` from the
   [latest release](https://github.com/ChristopherVR/kotor-coop/releases/latest).
   On Nexus, extract the Main file ZIP to find the same setup program.
2. **Close KOTOR and run setup.** It finds your GOG or Steam copy, or lets you choose the folder.
   Allow the firewall rule if you want to host. Install through setup, not Vortex.
3. **Start KOTOR → Co-op → Host.** Use an existing save, or a new game after the first autosave.
4. **Your friend chooses Co-op → Connect**, selects the host, or enters the host's address.
   On the first join, the normal character-creation screen lets them make their own character.

Both players need **the same co-op version**. Start with matching game mods too. Internet hosting
may need port forwarding or a tunnel; the mod does not supply a relay server. See the
[host/join guide](https://christophervr.github.io/kotor-coop/play.html).

While connected, load the save called **Co-op** to resume your session. Your own autosave is
backed up as **Autosave before co-op**. Press **Enter** to chat and **~** for the console.
Press **F9** for connection help, copying your hosting address, retrying, resuming hosting,
leaving co-op or creating a support report. Copying an address does not prove that friends
outside your network can reach it; internet hosting may still need router or tunnel setup.

<details>
<summary>ZIP installation, Windows prompts and Linux packages</summary>

Prefer the plain Windows ZIP? Extract it into its own folder (not over the game) and run
`KotorCoop.Agent.exe`. It provides the same installation flow. The files are not code-signed,
so SmartScreen may warn. Release assets include `SHA256SUMS.txt` to verify your download;
report antivirus detections rather than adding exclusions.

The Linux / Steam Deck tarball includes `install.sh` for Proton or Wine. The Linux installer
is tested; Linux gameplay remains unverified. See [Steam and Linux](#steam-and-linux).

</details>

## What works, and where the limits are

| Feature | What you can do | Current limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Join and reconnect | Host from the game menu, join as your own character, leave and return | Separate-PC internet and automatic router setup need wider testing |
| Explore and travel | See each other, change areas, take the same planet trip | Brief position correction can happen after loading |
| Combat | Fight the same enemies with your own gear; enemies scale for a group | Staged fights are tested; full-campaign balance is not verified |
| Dialogue and story | Watch the same conversation; share quest and journal progress | One speaker chooses replies; recent dialogue fixes still need ordinary retesting |
| Inventory and shops | Keep personal backpacks and credits; share quest items and merchant stock | The host controls companion equipment; simultaneous container access needs retesting |
| Saves and recovery | Save/load in co-op and automatically rejoin after a game disconnect | Unsaved progress can be lost; a host helper crash requires hosting again |
| Minigames | Play Pazaak, swoop racing and turret encounters | One player plays; everyone else waits |
| Larger parties | Connect up to eight players; group travel and combat have been demonstrated | Start with two; three-to-eight-player campaign reliability is experimental |

These are summaries of recorded results, not a promise that every scene works. **Recent fixes
for dialogue over equipment menus, Trask disappearing, container access, save-name input,
subtitles/skipping and the post-save enemy banner still need ordinary in-game confirmation.**
A complete two-player campaign, the full ending chain and independent-PC/Steam invite scenarios
remain unverified unless specifically recorded.

[Detailed player limitations](docs/limitations.md) ·
[Engineering status and evidence](docs/status-engineering.md) ·
[Current release checklist](docs/RELEASE-READINESS.md)

## What you need

- **KOTOR 1 v1.0.3**, GOG or Steam, lawfully owned by each player. KOTOR 2 is not supported.
- **64-bit Windows** for the verified gameplay baseline. Linux/Steam Deck packaging is available.
- Matching co-op versions, matching game mods for your first session, and backed-up saves.
- For two instances on one PC: separate game folders and at least one GOG copy; Steam allows
  only one running copy. The baseline captures use the game's 800×600 view; full widescreen
  and replacement-menu compatibility remain under test.

## About the project

This began as an experiment in adding co-op to a 2003 game through memory scanning and engine
hooks, without its source code. The design takes inspiration from Elden Ring's Seamless Co-op:
one player hosts, friends drop in, and each keeps their own character. The reverse-engineering
notes and unsuccessful experiments are kept alongside the code for other modders to use.

<details>
<summary>The experiment, how it grew, and other KOTOR co-op projects</summary>

## Where this came from

This project did not start as a mod. It started as a question: **how far can you take a 2003 game with
nothing but memory scanning and hooking, and no source code and no engine access?**

KOTOR has no networking layer for its story mode at all, and the community's long-standing answer was
that co-op is impossible without the executable's source. So the early versions did the obvious
experiment. A separate program attached to the running game, found the player's position in memory by
scanning for values and diffing snapshots, read it, and wrote the other player's position back. That
moved what the renderer drew but not what the simulation knew, so the "other player" had no collision
and could not be hit or talked to. The interesting part was everything we had to learn to fix that:

- **Finding things without symbols.** Signature scans against the *running* process (the executable on
  disk is packed, so the bytes in `.text` are not the bytes that execute), value-diff scans, and
  pointer paths from static globals. See [docs/FINDING-OFFSETS.md](docs/FINDING-OFFSETS.md) and
  [docs/re/](docs/re/).
- **Driving the engine instead of poking it.** Raw memory writes leave derived state stale, so the plugin
  spawns real creatures and moves them through the engine's own object system, the same calls a script
  would make. The notes on what those calls are, and the ones that crashed, are in
  [docs/research/](docs/research/README.md).
- **Hooks, kept to a minimum.** A small native plugin loaded as `dinput8.dll` (the game loads it by
  itself, so the executable on disk is never modified) installs a handful of hooks: one per frame, one
  in the main loop (which also runs at the menu) and one on the developer console's command interpreter.
  Everything else is calls into the engine.
- **A lot of trial and error.** The research directory is a lab notebook: roughly 150 write-ups of what
  worked, what crashed and why, kept because the dead ends are as useful as the findings.

The co-op mod is a **side effect** of that experiment. Once the avatars were real objects the engine
treated like any other creature, sharing doors, dialogue, combat, journals and saves became a series of
solvable problems, and at some point it turned into something people could actually play.

Because of that history, the codebase is unusual: an x86 NativeAOT C# plugin inside the game, an x64
helper that talks to it over a shared memory block, a UDP star topology with the host as authority, and a
large amount of reverse-engineering knowledge written down alongside the code. If you want to learn how
KOTOR's engine ticks, the documentation may be worth more than the mod.

### Elden Ring-style "seamless"

The design target was Elden Ring's Seamless Co-op, not a traditional multiplayer lobby. Concretely:

- **No server to run.** Whoever is hosting is just a player; everyone talks to the host.
- **Drop in, drop out.** Join a running game, leave, rejoin. A crash on either side is survived.
- **Your character is yours.** You keep your own character, backpack and credits, and the shared world
  (doors, containers, quests, enemies, the map) is the host's.
- **The game stays the game.** You play the normal campaign in the normal UI; the mod adds a Co-op
  button, a chat line and a console verb or two.

[docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) compares what Elden Ring gives its co-op mod for free with
what had to be built here for KOTOR.

## Other KOTOR co-op projects

We are not the only ones working on this, and **the other projects may well turn out better in the long run.**
Two more recent ones we know of:

- [**masterxxstabs/KOTOR-COOP**](https://github.com/masterxxstabs/KOTOR-COOP): a persistent dedicated
  server that keeps the campaign state alive when nobody is playing, with a launcher and server browser
  and a client DLL. A "world that persists" design rather than a "drop in on a friend" one.
- [**McChaffeeFAF/kotor-coop**](https://github.com/McChaffeeFAF/kotor-coop): a fork of the
  reone open-source engine reimplementation with online co-op.
  Because it owns the engine, it does not depend on hooking the original executable.

Both have clear advantages over this project's approach. A server-authoritative design and a re-implemented
engine do not have to fight the original executable's internals, so they can in principle be more stable and
easier to maintain. Hooking the real game, as we do, gets you the original game and its mod ecosystem
exactly as it is, at the price of brittleness (a single exact executable version, a lot of engine
state to keep consistent, and crashes when we guess wrong). If one of those projects does what you need,
use it. This one is open source so that anything useful in it, including the reverse-engineering
notes, can be reused by them or by anyone else.

(Descriptions are from each project's public page and may be out of date; check them directly.)

</details>

## Steam and Linux

The Steam copy is the same game wrapped in a copy-protection layer, so installing is identical. Steam-to-Steam
and Steam-to-GOG sessions both work. Two copies on one PC need at least one GOG copy. The optional Steam
friends-list "Join Game" invite is explained in [docs/research/steam-support.md](docs/research/steam-support.md).

The release also carries a Linux tarball with `install.sh`, a bash port of the installer for the Windows
game running under Proton or Wine (including Steam Deck). It prints the launch option you need. The
installer is tested on Linux; gameplay on Linux is not a verified configuration. See
[docs/research/proton.md](docs/research/proton.md).

## What the mod changes

- It adds its files beside `swkotor.exe` (`dinput8.dll`, the plugin, `coop.ini`, a `coop-mods` folder, logs).
  The game executable is not changed. If another mod already uses `dinput8.dll` (ReShade, an ASI loader),
  the installer sets the two up side by side automatically.
- It turns on the game's cheat console setting (`EnableCheats=1` in `swkotor.ini`); the original file is kept
  as `swkotor.ini.kcoop-orig` and uninstall restores it.
- It keeps your own autosave as "Autosave before co-op" (the two most recent are kept) before co-op uses the
  Auto Save slot, adds a "Co-op" save and `saves\kotorcoop-character.*` for your co-op character.
- **Uninstall** from Windows "Installed apps", or `KotorCoop.Agent.exe uninstall`. It removes the mod files,
  logs and remembered address, and keeps `coop.ini`, the "Co-op" save and your co-op character.

Updates preserve `coop.ini`. Everything lives in that one commented file
(`profiles/coop.ini.example`; the full list is [docs/CONFIG.md](docs/CONFIG.md)). For a bug report,
double-click `KotorCoop.CollectLogs.cmd` or run `KotorCoop.Agent.exe logs` to make a support zip.
You can also choose **Create support report** in the Co-op browser. Open **READ-ME-FIRST.txt**
inside the ZIP before sharing: recognized addresses, paths and credentials are removed from
text automatically, but chat and other players' names may remain. Nothing is uploaded, and
your original logs are unchanged. The report includes a crash summary, not raw stack memory.
Problems are covered in [docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md](docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md).

## For developers

### Build from source

Use **.NET SDK 10.0.113**, pinned by `global.json`. Release dependency notices audit
its bundled runtime version; newer SDK patches must be audited before changing the pin.

Needs the .NET 10 SDK and the Visual Studio 2022 MSVC x86 C++ tools (for the plugin and the chain loader).

```powershell
dotnet build KotorCoop.slnx                     # agent, session, protocol, memory, tests
dotnet test  tests\KotorCoop.Tests
pwsh src\KotorCoop.Plugin\build.ps1 -Install    # plugin + agent + overrides into the GOG default folder
pwsh tools\package.ps1                          # dist\kotor-coop-<version>-{setup.exe,windows.zip,linux.tar.gz}
```

`package.ps1` builds `setup.exe` when [Inno Setup 6](https://jrsoftware.org/isinfo.php) is installed
(`winget install JRSoftware.InnoSetup`). The solution build does not compile the plugin; use `build.ps1`.
To drive two instances unattended on one machine, see `tools/demo.ps1` and `tools/verify.ps1`.
The full build, test, live-rig and release reference is [docs/CONTRIBUTING.md](docs/CONTRIBUTING.md).

### How it works

```
the game (unmodified on disk): a small in-process plugin adds a few hooks and a shared memory block
       <--- shared memory, found by signature scan --->
the agent (a separate program): reads your character, writes everyone else's, talks to the
other players over the network
       <--- UDP: positions, items, enemies, flags, journal --->
```

Everyone talks only to the host; authority is explicit (your character is yours, enemies are the host's).
Full design: [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md).

### Releases

Every push to `main` that passes CI automatically increments the release version and publishes
`setup.exe`, the Windows zip, the Linux tarball and `SHA256SUMS.txt` on GitHub, then uploads the
installer to Nexus Mods and updates the mod page's version. Each published release is marked
**Latest** on GitHub so it appears in the repository sidebar. Beta status remains in the version
name and release notes. The release checklist is
[docs/RELEASE-READINESS.md](docs/RELEASE-READINESS.md). The Nexus Mods listing text and upload steps are
in [nexus/](nexus/README.md).

### Documentation map

- [docs/limitations.md](docs/limitations.md): what works and what doesn't, for players.
- [docs/status-engineering.md](docs/status-engineering.md): the same list with the evidence behind each status.
- [docs/CONTRIBUTING.md](docs/CONTRIBUTING.md): build, test, the live rig, CI and releases, code conventions.
- [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md): the design and why it looks like this.
- [docs/CONFIG.md](docs/CONFIG.md) and [docs/CONSOLE.md](docs/CONSOLE.md): every `coop.ini` key and console verb.
- [docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md](docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md): common problems and causes.
- [docs/FINDING-OFFSETS.md](docs/FINDING-OFFSETS.md), [docs/re/](docs/re/) and
  [docs/research/](docs/research/README.md): how engine addresses were found and what each feature learned.
- [docs/PLAYTEST.md](docs/PLAYTEST.md) and [docs/live-verification.md](docs/live-verification.md): what only a person at the keyboard can prove.
- [tools/README.md](tools/README.md): what every helper script does.

## Contributing

Issues and pull requests are welcome; start with [docs/CONTRIBUTING.md](docs/CONTRIBUTING.md). When reporting
a bug include the release version, GOG or Steam, player count and steps to reproduce, and review logs before
sharing (remove addresses, passwords and personal paths). Never attach game files. Security reports:
[SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

# Architecture

## The shape of the problem

Seamless Co-op for Elden Ring is not a netcode implementation. Elden Ring already replicates
phantoms; the mod removes FromSoftware's restrictions on that replication and adds a
supplementary channel for world state — which is why one person could build it. KOTOR has no
replication layer at all, so this project has to supply one:

| Layer                                    | Elden Ring          | KOTOR                        |
| ---------------------------------------- | -------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Transport and session                    | exists, repurposed   | built here                   |
| Avatar replication (position, animation) | exists, unlocked     | built here                   |
| World progression sync                   | added by the mod     | built here                   |
| A remote entity the engine can draw      | exists (phantoms)    | built here, by the plugin    |

The fourth row used to be the honest boundary of this project: memory-poking a position
field moves what the renderer shows but not what the simulation knows about, so a body
poked into existence that way has no collision and cannot be hit. The plugin closes that gap
by injecting into the process and driving the engine's own object system — spawning a real
`CSWSCreature` through `Odyssey.SpawnCreature` (the engine's own NWScript `CreateObject`,
called on the game thread) and stepping it every frame through the same movement/animation
calls a script would use. See `docs/re/spawn.md`/`docs/re/engine-movement.md` and "The
plugin" below.

## Process topology

```
   swkotor.exe (x86, player A)                        swkotor.exe (x86, player B)
   dinput8.dll proxy (KotorCoop.Plugin)                dinput8.dll proxy
        |  SharedBlock (shared memory, signature-      |  SharedBlock
        |  scanned, not IPC)                           |
   KotorCoop.Agent.exe (x64, external)             KotorCoop.Agent.exe (x64, external)
   KotorGameBridge <-> CoopAgent <-> CoopClient/Host    KotorGameBridge <-> CoopAgent <-> CoopClient/Host
        \                                               /
         \_______________ UDP star relay ______________/
                    (host is also a peer)
```

Each `swkotor.exe` loads the plugin as a `dinput8.dll` proxy the game itself resolves — no
game file is modified. The proxy is chainable: it forwards the six dinput8 exports to
`coop.ini`'s `dinput8_next`, else to the entry after itself in `dinput8.chain`, else to the
system DLL (`Exports.cs`). When another mod already owns the `dinput8.dll` name, the
`KotorCoop.Loader` wrapper (one C file, no CRT) takes the name instead, loads every
`dinput8.chain` entry and forwards to the first proxy among them — the plugin, installed as
`KotorCoop.Plugin.dll`. Because of this the plugin locates the game directory from
`swkotor.exe`'s own module path, never from its own file name. The plugin allocates a block of unmanaged memory
(`SharedBlock`/`SharedBlockView`) and never talks to the network; the external agent attaches
with `OpenProcess`, finds that block by scanning for a signature, and pumps it every tick.
Only the agent speaks UDP; one instance hosts (a star relay, not a mesh).

## Project layering

```
KotorCoop.Agent / KotorCoop.MockGame        entry points (x64)
        |
KotorCoop.Session       CoopAgent, CoopHost, CoopClient, SnapshotBuffer, pumps
        |
KotorCoop.Memory        ProcessMemory, PatternScanner, GameProfile, KotorGameBridge
        |
KotorCoop.Protocol      PacketCodec, Packets, PlayerState, Vector3f
```

Dependencies point one way, Protocol outward to Agent/MockGame. `IGameBridge` is the only
seam that knows about a specific game; `ProfileGameBridge` is the JSON-profile
implementation the mock harness and (through `KotorGameBridge`) the real game both drive
through. `PacketCodec.cs` and `Packets.cs` are themselves split into per-feature partials —
`PacketCodec.<Feature>.cs` and `Packets/<Feature>Packets.cs`, one per wire channel (avatar
state, flags, items, journal, party, dialogue, combat, movies, chat...), mirroring
`PacketType.cs`. Adding a channel means adding a partial, not growing the existing ones.

`KotorCoop.Plugin` (x86, NativeAOT) cannot reference any of the above — different bitness —
but shares 5 dependency-free Protocol files by SOURCE via its `.csproj`'s `<Compile
Include>` block: `DialogueFollowClock.cs`, `DialogueFollowMachine.cs`,
`DialogueNodeFollower.cs`, `DialogueAutoJoinRule.cs`, `ContainerAnimationEdges.cs`. Any
wire-shaped rule the plugin needs to evaluate identically to the agent has to be pure and
dependency-free enough to live in Protocol and be pulled in this way.

## Memory access

External, not injected, from the agent's side (`OpenProcess` + `ReadProcessMemory`/
`WriteProcessMemory`). `KotorGameBridge` is `KotorGameBridge.cs` plus 18
`KotorGameBridge.<Concern>.cs` partials (Attach, Player, Party, Items, Doors, Enemies,
Journal, Travel, Cheats, Encounters, WorldState, ContainerLoot, GroundItems, Placeables,
Menu, Dialogue, Helpers, PluginBlock); `PluginBlock` mirrors `SharedBlock`'s `[FieldOffset]`s
field-for-field on the agent side.

Details that still matter: pointers in a 32-bit target are 4 bytes even from a 64-bit agent
(`ProcessMemory.PointerSize` follows `IsWow64Process`); `Process.Modules` fails
cross-bitness, so `EnumProcessModulesEx(LIST_MODULES_ALL)` is used instead; freed memory
keeps its contents, so a scan can anchor on a dead copy — the plugin's block carries a
`Heartbeat` dword the agent watches for exactly this reason; and discovery scans by
snapshot diff, not enumeration (`ValueScanner`), since diffing two ~120 MB snapshots gives a
complete first pass at fixed cost instead of enumerating tens of millions of candidates.
`KotorGameBridge` re-resolves the plugin block after repeated read failures, since a save
load or transition can free what it anchored on.

## The plugin (`KotorCoop.Plugin`, x86, NativeAOT)

Runs inside `swkotor.exe`. Two threads, strictly divided: a worker thread only touches the
shared block; the frame hook runs on the game's own thread and is the only place engine
calls happen — the engine is not reentrant.

**Three hook points**, installed in `PluginHost.Startup.cs` in a fixed, commented order
(`InstallCrashProbe` first — a fault during startup must be diagnosable like one during
play — then the shared block, `ConstructControllers`, then `InstallHooks`; every install
carries its own comment saying why its position matters, e.g. the block must exist before
`FuncInterpHook`, which needs `_view` to publish into):

- **`FrameHook`** — an IAT patch on the import slot holding `GDI32!SwapBuffers`
  (`0x0073D00C`), the last thing in a frame after both engine `MainLoop`s. Drives the
  per-frame callback (`OnFrame`) that runs every world controller; dormant at the main menu,
  where the looping menu movie routes the swap through Bink instead (`docs/re/frame-hook.md`).
- **`MainLoopHook`** — a call-site rewrite on `CClientExoApp::MainLoop` inside `WinMain`,
  which fires at the menu too. Drives `MenuFrame`: the Co-op button, server browser,
  password prompt, and (only while `FrameHook` is visibly stalled behind a load screen) a
  fallback ~10 Hz pump of the world pipeline.
- **`FuncInterpHook`** — an inline detour on the developer console's command interpreter
  (`FuncInterp 0x0044C1F0`). A co-op verb is published to the block and swallowed before the
  engine sees it (no "function not found"); anything else tail-calls the original
  interpreter, so the `~` console works at the menu too, independent of the frame hook.

**The per-frame schedule** (`PluginHost.Frame.cs`'s `OnFrame`) is one long, explicitly
ordered method, not a generic "list of controllers to iterate" — each call is preceded by a
comment saying why it precedes or follows its neighbour (e.g.
`Odyssey.CloseClientWorldIfServerModuleGone` runs before anything else touches the world,
because the engine's own map-init code dereferences a freed server module with no null
check; staging cheats run dead last, on state every earlier pass has already settled).
`PluginHost.Controllers.cs` constructs the ~35 per-frame controllers in one place, in the
same order as before the split — that order is incidental; the call order in `Frame.cs` is
what is load-bearing.

**`PluginEvents`** is a static, dependency-free typed event hub (`WorldLoadObserved`,
`ModuleTransitionStarted`, `ServerModuleGone`, `DialogueStarted`/`Ended`,
`LocalCombatEngagementChanged`, `PeerSlotSpawned`/`Destroyed`, `SessionConnected`/
`Released`) raised synchronously on the game thread, from the point each condition is
already detected — it adds a notification, not a new detection — with every raise
per-subscriber exception-isolated so one throwing subscriber cannot fail-fast the game from
inside the `[UnmanagedCallersOnly]` frame hook. Being dependency-free, it also compiles
directly into the test project.

**`PluginHost.SessionLifecycle.cs`** turns a session's presence in the block
(`Command == CommandSpawnAndDrive`) into engine state changes both ways:
`PumpSessionLifecycle` raises `SessionConnected`/`SessionReleased` on the edge, and every
controller holding engine or GUI state does its own teardown from `ReleaseSession` rather
than a second hand-written list — a structural fix for a bug class where per-field teardown
kept missing one field. `DrainSessionSpawns` destroys everything the session spawned across
several frames, since the engine refuses a destroy call while its script VM is mid-call.

### The `SharedBlock` contract

An explicit-layout (`[FieldOffset]`) struct allocated with `VirtualAlloc` (a fixed address
the agent can scan for) inside `swkotor.exe`. Split by concern (`SharedBlock.Session.cs`,
`.Combat.cs`, `.Dialogue.cs`, `.Items.cs`, `.Party.cs`, `.World.cs`, `.Browser.cs`,
`.Cheats.cs`, plus the base file), with a matching `SharedBlockView.<Concern>.cs` split for
the typed accessors both the plugin and the tests use. `KotorGameBridge.PluginBlock.cs`
mirrors the same offsets on the agent's x64 side — the two halves cannot share a type
(different bitness), so every offset is written twice on purpose, and a mismatch reads as
"plugin not found" rather than a crash.

`Magic` + `Version` + a guard dword form a 16-byte scan signature; bumping `Version`
intentionally severs old agents from a new plugin rather than letting them silently
misinterpret a moved field. `ItemHarnessTests`/`CheatKindSyncTests` assert the version and
cheat-kind numbering agree between the plugin's `SharedBlock.cs` and the agent's
`CheatKinds` mirror at build time — the two are transcribed by hand and drift is otherwise
silent.

## The agent (`KotorCoop.Agent`, x64)

`Program.cs` (45 lines) is pure routing: parse `AgentOptions`, dispatch to one
`Commands/<Verb>Command.cs` file per CLI verb. `AgentComposition.Compose` is the composition
root a live `agent run` uses: resolve coop.ini, compute the install's content digest, build
`AgentSettings`/`SessionManager`, wire the `CoopCommandDispatcher`, and wire logging so every
session event and console reply reach a file an unattended run can read.

**`CoopCommandDispatcher`** is the single command surface for the whole session — CLI
`--host`/`--join`, the in-game `~` console, the main-menu Co-op button and the server
browser panel all resolve to the same `Dispatch(CoopCommand)` call. `Partial` by area
(`.Connect.cs`, `.Session.cs`, `.SaveLoad.cs`, `.Items.cs`, `.Movies.cs`, `.Doors.cs`,
`.Effects.cs`, `.Cheats.cs`, `.Browser.cs`, `.Announcers.cs`, `.Diagnostics.cs`) with a
`Dictionary<CoopCommandKind, Action<CoopCommand>>` built once; the base file owns the 150 ms
tick loop, that table, and the shared staging-cheat request/answer channel (only one cheat
in flight at a time — the plugin has one 96-byte reply slot).

`CoopAgent` (612 lines) is the scheduler that joins the two halves: read the local player
out of the game, hand it to the session, take the session's view of everyone else, write it
back. The per-feature work lives in `KotorCoop.Session.Pumps` (`BarkPump`, `TransitionPump`
+ `.Movies`/`.Travel`, `LootPump`, `DialoguePump`, `PartyPump`, `CombatPump` +
`.PhantomAndEffects`/`.Enemies`, `LivenessPump`, `TriggerPump`, `PausePump`, `DeathPump`,
`WorldStatePump`); `PumpOnce` owns only the schedule and the module/peer bookkeeping its
typed events (`ModuleChanged`, `WorldAdopted`, `PeerJoined`, `PeerLeft`, `LocalStateRead`)
are raised from.

**Three cadences**, all wall-clock gated, not tick-counted — tying scan rate to send rate
was a real, measured bug: raising the tick rate multiplied how often the expensive scans
ran, and positions took 3.5-7.4 seconds to cross. **Every tick** (`DefaultTickRate = 30`
Hz): local player read/publish, position, pause, shared combat state, death arbitration
(checked against every peer, not the module-filtered set, or "everyone is down" can go true
while a peer is alive elsewhere), and, when fast-pathed, dialogue/party. **Every
`CombatPumpIntervalMs`** (150 ms default): enemy census, phantom damage, peer effects,
materialised loot, and (unless fast-pathed) dialogue/party/interaction locks/container
state — fast enough that a mirrored enemy's movement reads as movement, not a
once-a-second lurch. **Every `HeavyPumpIntervalMs`** (~1 Hz): items, progression, world
state, journal, doors, placeables, container loot — full memory scans, deliberately rare.

`SessionManager` owns a session's lifecycle (`Connect`/`Disconnect`/`Reconnect`/`Poll`) so the
console's `connect`/`disconnect`/`reconnect` can tear down and restand a session without
restarting the process, exposing `SessionPhase` through a `PhaseChanged` event raised from the
single `SetPhase` helper every transition already goes through.

`ConsoleCommand` (shared by the console and the dashboard) is a declarative `VerbSpec` table
built into a `Dictionary<string, ...>` once; each verb's argument grammar lives in a small
parse method inside the `ConsoleCommand.<Area>.cs` file for its area, and `Parse` itself
only strips an optional `coop`/`/coop` prefix and does the table lookup.

`ICoopSession` is a composite of 16 role interfaces (peer, lifecycle, flags, items, enemies,
damage, triggers, barks, movies, capabilities, party, dialogue, interaction locks, chat,
loot, journal), mirroring `IGameBridge` in `KotorCoop.Memory` (`IPlayerBridge` carries the 5
members with no sane default — attach status, read local state, write remote peers, clear
co-op state; every other interface default-implements, gated by a `Supports*` flag, so a
bridge that cannot do something simply doesn't override it). `CoopHost`/`CoopClient` are
`partial` per feature (`CoopHost.<Feature>.cs`/`CoopClient.<Feature>.cs`, one pair per wire
channel) with a `Dictionary<PacketType, PacketHandler>` built once in the constructor, and
`Channels/RelayQueue<T>` is the shared "receive locally, relay to everyone but the sender"
inbox/outbox idiom several unreliable channels used to hand-roll separately.

## Wire protocol, session and interpolation

Carried over from the pre-refactor design, still accurate. Binary, little-endian,
hand-written, with a 4-byte header (2-byte magic, 1-byte version, 1-byte type) so foreign
traffic on the port costs almost nothing to reject. Reads never throw on malformed input:
`PacketReader` sets a `Failed` flag and yields defaults, the codec returns `null`, and a
corrupt datagram is simply dropped — a test fires 40 random datagrams at a live host and
asserts the session survives.

**Packet budget.** `ProtocolConstants.MaxPacketSize = 1400` bytes (inside the smallest
common path MTU so nothing fragments). Raised once already, from 1200: a full 8-peer lobby
with every string field at its cap came to ~1265 bytes and was silently dropped once a
session filled up, because the guard test measured a peer with no equipment. Per-field caps
(`MaxNameLength = 24`, `MaxModuleLength = 32`, `MaxTagLength = 32`) keep the worst case under
the limit; `FullPeerSnapshotFitsInOneDatagram` guards it.

**Star relay.** Clients send only to the host, which broadcasts the combined world and is a
participant, not a spectator — peer 1, its own avatar in the same snapshot as everyone else's.

**Two reliability classes.** Avatar state is unreliable and rate-limited
(`DefaultTickRate = 30` Hz) — a dropped position update is superseded next tick, so
retransmitting it would only add latency. World flags, items, journal, loot and dialogue
grants are reliable: `ReliableFlagSender` retransmits until acknowledged, then gives up
after a bounded number of attempts rather than leaking into a dead link.

**Flag versioning.** Every flag change bumps a counter the host stamps into every
`WorldSnapshot` (4 bytes/tick); a client whose version differs requests a full flag
snapshot, rate-limited. `EventFlagStore` also deduplicates by `(originPeer, sequence)` in a
bounded ring, since UDP retransmission means the same op can arrive twice and a toggle
applied twice is a toggle undone.

**Interpolation.** Remote peers render at `now - DefaultInterpolationDelayMs` (80 ms, just
over two tick intervals on a LAN), interpolated between the two bracketing snapshots — never
extrapolated, avoiding extrapolation-based rubber-banding. Facing interpolates along the
shortest arc; a module change is a teleport, not motion, snapping rather than dragging an
avatar through the space between two areas; and a peer in a different module (or the
engine's own minigame mode) is not written into the game at all — KOTOR loads one module at
a time, so a peer elsewhere has no meaningful position in your copy of it.

## The mock harness and testing

`KotorCoop.MockGame` exists because "does the co-op stack work" and "have we found KOTOR's
offsets" are separate questions, and conflating them makes both unanswerable. It allocates a
player structure in unmanaged memory (`GameStateBlock`), marks it with a magic signature, and
renders (`MockRenderer`) whatever remote avatars appear in it (`MockWorld`). The agent
attaches by PID and finds the block by scanning for the signature — exactly as it does
against the real game — so the scanner, pointer arithmetic, and reads/writes under test are
the production ones; only the game is faked, and rendering deliberately reads from the
memory block rather than the session, so a remote avatar only appears if genuinely written
in from outside.

`tests/KotorCoop.Tests`, xUnit, parallelisation disabled assembly-wide
(`AssemblyInfo.cs`) because `MemoryBridgeTests`/`ValueScannerTests` self-attach to the test
process and full address-space sweeps against your own runtime are unsafe: measured live,
sweeping a *separate* process (`PatternScanner.ScanAll`, `ValueScanner.TakeSnapshot`,
`FindPointersTo`) costs nothing (120 MB captured in 0.1 s, diffed in 0.3 s, repeatedly); run
against the calling process itself, the same code intermittently kills the .NET runtime with
`0x80131506` (`COR_E_EXECUTIONENGINE`) inside `coreclr.dll` — reading one's own GC heap
through `ReadProcessMemory` in a tight loop is unsupported, and a snapshot's own byte arrays
live inside the address space it is capturing, so each capture compounds the last. Neither
applies to the real tool (the agent is a separate process from the game); the tests that
attach to the test host now anchor on a known address or scope the sweep to a bounded
window, with the unbounded paths exercised only against a spawned child process in
`ExternalTargetTests`. Some suites also bind real UDP ports, including
`ProtocolConstants.DefaultPort`, so two concurrent test runs on one machine can flake
`CoopCommandDispatcherTests` — a port-collision failure is a machine-contention artifact,
worth one rerun before treating it as a regression.

What each group proves: **codec** tests round-trip, truncate, reject a version and foreign
traffic, and guard the datagram budget; **interpolation** covers midpoint accuracy,
clamping, module snapping, shortest-arc facing, out-of-order/NaN rejection, pruning;
**flags/items/journal/loot** cover version bumps, duplicate-op suppression, cross-peer
sequence independence, retransmit backoff; **memory** tests allocate a real block, write
remote peers into it and read them back through genuine pointer-chain indirections;
**external-target** tests spawn `KotorCoop.MockGame` as a separate process and sweep its
address space for the signature — the production configuration; **session** tests run real
`CoopHost`/`CoopClient` over loopback UDP (connection, bidirectional visibility, movement,
flag sync both ways, three-way relay, survival under random garbage); **dispatcher/console**
tests exercise `CoopCommandDispatcher`/`ConsoleCommand` directly rather than only through a
live game.

**The plugin compile-include trick.** The plugin is NativeAOT win-x86 and cannot be
referenced from the (x64) test project, but its pure-arithmetic files are exactly the ones
most worth testing directly rather than re-implementing their rules in a test (a mirrored
copy of a rule is a rule that can drift). `KotorCoop.Tests.csproj` pulls in ~50
dependency-free plugin files with `<Compile Include="..\..\src\KotorCoop.Plugin\X.cs"
Link="Plugin\X.cs" />` — `DamageDealtTable`, `DamageOwedLedger`, every `SharedBlock*`/
`SharedBlockView*` file, `PluginEvents`, and every standalone `*Rule.cs`/`*Ledger.cs`/
`*Table.cs`. Only genuinely dependency-free files qualify — anything touching
`SharedBlockView`'s unsafe pointer plumbing, `Odyssey`, or an engine call will not compile in
a 64-bit host. A new pure-logic plugin file worth testing directly means one more
`<Compile Include>` line, not a reinvented copy of its rule in the test project.

## Engine-write rules

Distilled from `docs/re/` (`object-model.md`, `engine-movement.md`, `rendering.md`,
`spawn.md`, `frame-hook.md`), `docs/research/` (indexed at `docs/research/README.md`), and
hard-won live-testing rounds; every write against `swkotor.exe` in this codebase follows
these:

- **Rebuild derived state after a field poke, don't just poke the field.** A raw write to a
  door's open-state byte moves the collision without telling the area
  (`CSWSArea::BudgeCreatures` does that); the engine's own `MoveToNextOpenState`/`OpenDoor`
  calls commit a change correctly.
- **Prefer object ids over raw pointers across time**, and dispatch through a vtable slot
  rather than a hardcoded call address. A pointer into a `CSWSCreature` can be freed and
  reused; an id resolved fresh through `CServerExoApp::GetGameObject` is what every
  controller here keys on, and `KotorGameBridge` revalidates its cached player pointer every
  tick. A creature's `animbase` override is reached through an adjustor thunk, not a flat
  function pointer, so guards along that path log what they actually saw.
- **Verify a researched offset live before shipping the write.** `docs/FINDING-OFFSETS.md`
  exists because a wrong offset reads plausible garbage and fails silently; every offset in
  `profiles/kotor1.json` and every `SharedBlock` field was confirmed against the running
  process, not inferred from disk bytes alone (the executable is packed). And `CExoString`
  lengths include the terminating null — cut at the first null when reading one out of engine
  memory; three separate bugs in this project's history came from treating the reported
  length as the character count.
- **Never dispatch an engine call while the script VM is mid-call.** `Odyssey.SpawnCreature`
  checks `CallStackSize == 0` before touching the routine table, and every destroy call in
  the plugin is retried across frames, because a declined call (VM busy) silently orphans
  whatever it was trying to remove otherwise.

## Where this stops

**KOTOR 2 is untouched.** Every offset here is verified against the retail GOG KOTOR 1 build
v1.0.3 specifically (no ASLR, disk bytes == memory bytes outside the packer stub); a KOTOR 2
port is a fresh reverse-engineering pass, not a config change.

Within KOTOR 1, what remains open — party-character switching, follow-AI stalls, local
companion combat, dialogue recruitment sync, swoop racing, creature-liveness
reconciliation — is tracked live in `docs/status-engineering.md` (and, in plain language, in
`docs/limitations.md`) rather than duplicated here, since that list changes with nearly every
round of live testing; each item links a dated write-up in `docs/research/`.

text:
# What works and what doesn't

This page is for someone who wants to play KOTOR 1 from the Endar Spire to the Star Forge with a
friend, and wants to know what to expect before starting. It is written for players. The
developer version, with test dates, logs and settings, is the
[evidence log](research/limitations-evidence-log-2026-10-02.md) and
[status-engineering.md](status-engineering.md).

**Where things stand.** Joining, exploring, fighting and talking have been played through on two
real copies of the game across the early game (the Endar Spire, Taris, Dantooine) and selected later
scenes (the Leviathan, Manaan, the dark-side temple, the Star Forge). Eight copies on one PC have
travelled and fought together. A complete start-to-finish campaign with two people has **not** been
played yet, so expect the odd rough edge in places nobody has tried.

This page was written for the v0.1 beta release.

**Beta warning.** Dialogue appearing over the host's equipment
menu and Trask disappearing on the joining player's screen have fixes awaiting ordinary
in-game retesting. Save-name input, container responsiveness, subtitles/skipping and the
enemy-sighted banner after saving also await confirmation. Historical **Works** results
below do not close these newer reports. Public distribution is still gated by the
[release checklist](RELEASE-READINESS.md), including legal review.

## How to read the status words

| Word | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **Works** | Watched working on two real copies of the game, more than once. |
| **Works, with a catch** | Works, but there is a real gap you will notice. The catch is spelled out. |
| **Not shared, by design** | The mod chooses not to do this, and says why. |
| **Untested** | Built, and the automatic tests pass, but nobody has watched it on a running game. Treat it as "probably". |
| **Not supported** | Don't do this. It can break the game, and that is a limit of the original game. |
| **Not a mod limitation** | The base game already behaves this way, with or without the mod. |

---

## Getting into a game together

| | Status | What to expect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starting from the game's own menu | **Works** | There is a **Co-op** button on the main menu. One player presses **Host**; the other picks the server and presses **Connect**. Nothing to launch by hand. |
| Your own character | **Works** | The first time you join, the normal character-creation screen opens and you make your character. That character comes with you every time you join, and your named single-player saves are not touched. While you are connected, the mod keeps a save called **Co-op** in your Load Game list; load that one, not Auto Save. Joining uses the Auto Save slot, so your own autosave is first kept as a save called **Autosave before co-op** (the two most recent are kept). If the game crashes during a co-op save, your own quick save is put back, or kept as **Recovered quicksave**. |
| Bringing your own backpack and credits | **Works** | Your items and credits stay yours. If you disconnect and come back, you get your own back, not your partner's. |
| Playing over the internet | **Works, with a catch** | Independent-PC internet play remains unverified. The built-in automatic port opening was tried on a home connection without success. The Co-op browser can copy the hosting address and show connection help; an address or local self-test does not establish outside reachability. Some networks still need manual port forwarding or an external tunnel. The host must allow the agent through Windows Firewall: setup asks "Allow friends to connect to games you host?" and Windows asks for permission, so say yes. If you skipped it, run setup again. There is no relay server. |
| GOG and Steam copies together | **Works** | Any mix. Two copies on one PC need at least one to be the GOG version. |
| Saving and loading while connected | **Works** | Either player can save or load, and the other one rejoins by itself in about 10 to 20 seconds. If the host loads a save while the other player is still watching the Endar Spire's opening movie, the other player rejoins as soon as the movie ends. |
| Reconnecting after a drop | **Works** | You come back into the shared world. If the mod cannot tell your world still matches, it reloads you into the host's world after about 15 seconds, keeping your character, backpack and credits. |
| Your partner quits to the menu | **Works** | Their character disappears and a line on screen says they are away. They reappear when they come back. |
| The host's game crashes | **Works** | Within about six seconds you are released to play on alone, and the mod reconnects when the host returns. |
| The host's helper process crashes | **Works, with a catch** | Restarting the helper does not restore the hosted session by itself. The host must choose **Host** or **F9 → Start/resume hosting** again before the joining player can reconnect. A replacement helper waiting in menu mode is not a recovered session. |
| Three or more players | **Works, with a catch** | Up to eight can connect. Three players made twelve area changes in half an hour, and eight copies travelled and fought a shared enemy together. A whole campaign, and every kind of fight at that size, has not been tried. |
| Different mods on each side | **Works, with a catch** | The mod compares installs when you connect and tells you on screen what differs and what it switched off because of it. Any difference in the game's core files switches things off cautiously, even a cosmetic one. Checking a large install can make startup slower. |
| KMRP graphics patch | **Gameplay untested** | Matching executable/patch inputs avoid false join refusals. Updated setup preserves Ultimate ASI Loader's required filename and repairs older renamed-loader installs. KMRP 1.5.1 startup failures were reproduced; the fixed layout reached the Co-op menu in six driver-enabled retests, including High FPS. Both players need matching updated builds/settings; multiplayer gameplay still needs a playtest. |
| Wrong mod version on one side | **Works** | Refused in about a second with a plain message such as "Your co-op mod version differs from the host's ... Both players need the same release." A wrong game version or password gets its own plain message too ("Wrong password. Ask the host for the password and try again."). |
| The host stops responding | **Works** | The mod retries automatically and stops after five minutes. Use **F9 → Retry last connection** once the host is hosting again, or **Leave co-op** to stop retrying. A restarted helper alone does not mean the host session has resumed. |

## Moving around the world

| | Status | What to expect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Walking through doors and area changes | **Works, with a catch** | Either player can lead and the other follows through the same loading screen. The catch: for about a second after arriving, your partner can appear in the wrong spot before snapping into place. |
| Flying to another planet | **Works** | Either player can choose the destination on the galaxy map and the other is taken along, movie and landing included. |
| Choosing your companions before leaving the ship | **Works** | The host picks. If the other player starts the departure, the host sees a "wants to leave, choose your party" message and picks. |
| Seeing each other | **Works** | Your partner is a real in-game character with their own face, armour and weapons, on the real floor, and on the minimap and map. |
| Companions following the party | **Works, with a catch** | Companions follow the host's game, and a companion left behind is gathered back automatically. A companion controlled by the other player moves exactly as that player's game says, not on its own. |
| The map | **Works** | The map reveals around your partner as well as you. |
| Chests and doors, and who opened them first | **Works** | If you both click the same chest, exactly one of you opens it. Loot goes to one of you, never both. |
| Loot on enemy bodies | **Works** | One copy for the party: whatever one of you takes from a body is gone for the other too. Set `corpse_loot = personal` if you would rather each find your own copy. |
| Doors and chests the story locks or closes again | **Works, with a catch** | Opening, closing, locking and unlocking reach the other player. The catch: a door or chest that the story itself locks again (for example in the Sith base) has not been watched yet. |
| Using the `warp` console command quickly in a row | **Not supported** | Several `warp`s in a row can crash the game. That is a bug in the original game, and real doors do not do it. |

## Fighting

| | Status | What to expect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cairn Sentinel arena boss | **Not yet verified in-game** | The optional boss now has a new stone-automaton appearance, animations and sounds. These have passed automated checks but have not been watched in the game with two players. Earlier tests of the previous boss design do not verify this replacement. |
| Fighting the same enemies | **Works** | Enemies have one health bar that you both damage. Kills, deaths and loot agree on both screens, for one boss or a room full. |
| Which player an enemy goes after | **Works** | An enemy turns on whoever is hurting it most and lets go of a player who is down. |
| Really fighting, not just watching | **Works** | Your own game runs up to three fights at once for real. Enemies beyond that are mirrored, and your hits still land. |
| Enemies splitting attention | **Works, with a catch** | An enemy the host hit first will turn on you once you have clearly out-damaged the host. The game's own AI can still pull it back to the host. Not every kind of fight has been checked. |
| Stuns, fear, poison and other effects | **Works, with a catch** | Twelve kinds of effect reach your partner's real character or the shared enemy, in both directions, and healing and curing reach your partner too. Catches: a medpac only heals the person using it, and Speed affects only the caster. |
| Sneaking | **Works** | An enemy cannot target a partner who is sneaking, and their stand-in turns see-through on your screen. |
| Companions in combat | **Works, with a catch** | A companion's gear and experience stay in step on both sides. A companion fighting for the *other* player in a fight away from the host is off unless you switch it on. |
| Mods that replace a companion | **Works, with a catch** | Such replacements reach the other player, and a replacement companion carries across a reload. A full run of such a mod's story has not been played. |
| Going down, being rescued, a full wipe | **Works, with a catch** | A downed player watches from a spectator camera and can be rescued by their partner or a companion. After a full wipe the host reloads and the other player recovers on its own, keeping their own character and gear. The catch: repeated rescues used to crash the host in some fights on Manaan (now fixed, and tested through about 150 rescues), but a clean game-over sequence has not been watched start to finish. |
| Enemies scale with the number of players | **Works** | With more than one player, enemies have more health and hit harder (two players: about half as much health again and slightly harder hits) and shops stock more. Alone, nothing changes. |
| Placing a mine yourself | **Works, with a catch** | Off by default; you turn it on in the settings. When on, your partner sees the mine where you put it and enemies set it off for both of you. |
| Experience and levelling | **Works, with a catch** | Kill and story experience are earned by both players' games at the same time. If you both start with the same amount, you stay level with each other. If one character is already ahead (for example you brought a higher-level character), they keep their lead: experience is matched up to the higher total, never added together, so a gain by the one in front does not lift the other. |
| The Endar Spire and early Taris duels | **Not a mod limitation** | The game's own tutorial stops anyone dropping below 1 hit point there, so nobody can be downed in those fights. |

## Talking to people

| | Status | What to expect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Conversations | **Works, with a catch** | One conversation at a time. Whoever starts it chooses the replies. To watch it live, the other player clicks the same person; scenes the game starts by itself (cutscenes, story conversations) pull both players in automatically. This is deliberate: two people steering one conversation would break the story. |
| Recruiting companions through conversation | **Works** | When the host recruits someone, they join both players' parties. All nine companions have arrived correctly this way. If the joining player leads a recruitment, the host's game replays the conversation's scripts the same way it does for any conversation, and we could not make it fail in testing (no stock recruiter other than Bastila could be set up for a joiner-led test), so we treat it as working. Report it if it ever doesn't. |
| Cutscenes | **Works** | They play on both screens, and if one moves a player to a new area the other follows. |
| The Star Forge solo duels (Bastila, Malak) | **Works, with a catch** | The player not in the duel is held in place and watches. The duels themselves have not been played through with two people. |

## The party, items and shops

| | Status | What to expect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Your inventory | **Works** | Your backpack is your own. What you pick up, buy, sell or craft stays yours. Quest items are the exception: they appear for both of you so the story keeps working. There is a setting to share one stash instead. |
| Your credits | **Works** | Your credits are your own. A credits reward from a conversation pays each of you the full amount. |
| Switching which party member you control | **Not shared, by design** | Only the host switches the active party member; everyone sees it. |
| Choosing the party before a departure | **Not shared, by design** | The "pick your party" screen belongs to the host. |
| Equipping a companion as the joining player | **Works, with a catch** | The host owns companion gear, so the joining player's companion Equipment screen closes with a note. Ask the host to equip them. |
| Merchants | **Works, with a catch** | Shop stock is shared: what one of you buys is gone for the other. What you buy and what you pay stay yours. The shared stock only updates while someone has the shop open. |
| Journal and quests | **Works** | Quest progress merges upward: whatever the furthest-along player has done, both have done. |
| Things an NPC remembers ("we've already talked") | **Works, with a catch** | The important ones reach the other player, including after a late join or a change of area. Not every minor flag in the game is shared. |

## Minigames

| | Status | What to expect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pazaak | **Works** | One player plays; the other is told they are waiting. |
| Swoop racing | **Works** | One player races and the other is held in place with a "waiting" line, then released a moment after the race ends. Checked on the Taris, Manaan and Tatooine tracks, with either player as the racer, including quitting or crashing mid-race. After a race started from a normally loaded game, shared state stayed on and nothing needed re-syncing. Shared state staying off after a race was seen only in test setups that jumped straight to the track, and could not be reproduced from a normal load. Experience works as described under Experience and levelling. |
| The Ebon Hawk turret ambush | **Works** | The player at the turrets fights for real; the other waits and is released when it is over. |

## Controls and interface

| | Status | What to expect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Keyboard and mouse | **Works** | Everything the game already does, plus `~` for the console and Enter to chat. |
| Connecting by typing an address | **Works** | Choose **Connect to an address...** at the bottom of the server list and type the address the host gave you. |
| Connection and recovery actions | **Untested** | The Co-op browser and F9 menu now include Retry last connection, Copy connection address, Connection help, Create support report, Start/resume hosting and Leave co-op. These new actions still need ordinary in-game confirmation on the packaged release. |
| Seeing that you are connected | **Works** | A line of text at the top left shows the connection and fades out when it is not needed. |
| Pausing | **Works, with a catch** | The pause key pauses both games. Opening a menu only pauses *your* game, but for a few seconds your character cannot be hit on your partner's screen. Stay in a menu too long and that protection lapses, so it is a cushion, not a way to sit out a fight. |

## Story paths

Each of these was played on two real copies of the game, usually jumping ahead with the developer
commands so the test reached the scene without replaying the whole story. The scene itself ran
through the game's own scripts and conversations.

| | Status | What to expect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Becoming a Jedi on Dantooine | **Works, with a catch** | Whoever talks to Master Dorak first chooses a path, as in single-player. The other player is then asked on their own screen to choose Guardian, Consular or Sentinel, so you can end up on different paths. Each player then gets a lightsaber in their own colour, with no duplicates. The catch: the long run from Taris to Dantooine that earns the training has not been played with two people. |
| Story-skip mods (Super Skip Taris, Jedi From The Start) | **Works, with a catch** | With the same mod files on both computers, the skipped story, journal and class choice carry across. Other mods' scripts are not certified. |
| The Leviathan | **Works, with a catch** | The capture, the cell conversation and the interrogation matched on both screens, the other player is held still while the host swaps to a rescuer, and a host reload brings them back. Not reached yet: the command deck, the escape and the Malak reveal. One crash of the joining player's game was seen in the original engine on one of three elevator rides to the next deck; it did not happen again and could not be reproduced, so it is treated as a one-off. |
| The dark-side temple | **Works** | Bastila's scene is run by the host's game whichever player starts it. If the joining player tries to start it, the request goes to the host, who starts it, and the joining player watches it play. A player who connects part-way through joins the conversation at the point it has reached. When the host takes the dark path, Bastila joins the host's party, Jolee and Juhani leave and turn hostile, and both players see the same thing. This was tested from a saved state at the temple rather than by playing up to it. In a few early test runs the joining player did not see the conversation; that did not happen on any later run and could not be reproduced, so it is treated as a one-off. |
| Manaan (the sea-floor trip) | **Works** | When the host goes underwater, the other player stays at the station, held still with a "waiting" line, and is released when the host returns. A host disconnect mid-trip does not strand them. If the joining player tries to start the airlock, the request is passed to the host instead, because starting it themselves crashed their game; the host then gets the airlock screen (if the host is in a fight it waits a few seconds and gives up). The star map and the control-station puzzle were skipped when testing. |
| Cutscenes and visions between areas | **Works, with a catch** | The Endar Spire escape, the dream, the Taris landing and the end credits played on both screens. The full ending chain and the final fights with two people have not been played. |
| Saving with your partner next to you | **Works** | Your partner's stand-in is removed while the game saves, so it is never written into your save. |

## Things that look like bugs but are not

- **Nobody can be knocked out in the Endar Spire.** That is the game's own tutorial rule.
- **The joining player's click on a Manaan airlock or on Bastila at the dark-side temple hands the
  scene to the host.** That is deliberate: the host runs those scenes so the story stays in one place.
- **A settings file from an old install keeps its old values.** The installer never overwrites your
  settings. Double-click setup previews any settings that still match older defaults and offers
  to update them, after making a backup; decline to keep yours. If something this page says is on
  seems off, compare with the packaged `KotorCoop.DEFAULTS.ini`.

## Still incomplete or not fully verified

These still need live testing or have unresolved failures from the checks so far:

- A friend on a different internet connection joining through the automatic port opening.
- The Windows firewall rule making the difference on a second real PC.
- Very long sessions: the longest was about three and a half hours with two copies.
- Full widescreen and replacement-menu compatibility. Co-op now follows the live button
  column and chooses a visible, non-overlapping slot. The supplied KOTOR Enhanced Menu and
  Controller Support v3.0 archive was checked on this PC with GOG 1.03. Cold 1280x720,
  1920x1080, 2560x1440 and 3840x2160 now retain their requested size, render Co-op, and accept clicks
  on the drawn Co-op, browser Cancel and Options/Graphics controls. The early resolution
  fallback and isolated-background mouse offsets are fixed. Co-op also rebinds when a
  resolution reload restores its old label. The 4K startup crash is fixed by preserving
  requested windowed mode. The 1024x768 → 1280x720 → 1024x768 round trip now keeps controls
  visible and clickable. This is **not full compatibility**: Enhanced still needs a restart
  to regenerate layout/fonts, so large reductions can leave old controls outside the viewport.
  The full 4K client check used a borderless window on a private desktop; ordinary decorated
  windows can be constrained by Windows. This PC does not advertise 3440x1440, which still
  falls back to 800x600. Steam, normal foreground input, exclusive fullscreen and physical controllers
  remain unverified. Geometry tests through 5120x1440 do not establish rendering there.
  If the button cannot fit, try **F9**. See the [evidence and remaining checks](research/menu-widescreen-compatibility.md).
- Parts of the story that were skipped when testing: the Manaan star map and control-station puzzle, the Leviathan command deck and escape, and a story script locking a door or chest again (the Sith base).
- A complete two-player campaign past Taris and through the ending.

If you try one of these and it works, or doesn't, that is the most useful bug report there is.
[PLAYTEST.md](PLAYTEST.md) lists each one with the exact steps, and `KotorCoop.Agent.exe logs`
makes a zip of logs to attach.
